How green fracking is depends on how it's done.

Regardless of method there are going to be earthquakes. Bedrock is being fractured, which destabilizes overlying rock. If you think that low magnitude earthquakes are bad for the environment then yes, fracking is always bad for the environment.

Now, on to my point.

Fracking is a term that describes fracturing rock using fluid pressure, then sucking out any liquids and gasses that are trapped in those rocks.

It is often used on a soft sedimentary rock called oil shale. Oil shale forms in deep marine (and sometimes lacustrian) environments. Plankton like plants and animals lived in the water, and when they died they sank to the bottom. The overlying water (since it's deep it's also oxygen poor) protects the dead organic matter from predation from aerobic bacteria. The organic matter is buried under sediment carried in from the continents and it is compacted over time. What this gets you is a mudrock that has a lot of organic matter in it's matrix that over time and with pressure turns into fossil fuels. Basically you have a solid rock that has liquid oil and hydrocarbon gasses trapped in it's matrix.

How do you get it out? You pulverize the rock and sort out the liquid and gas bits from the solid bits.

In this example an oil shale layer is identified, and it's location is determined by linking rock cores and using techniques such as shooting the ground with a big ass shotgun while really fucking expensive microphones are left lying on the ground. Basically we create a soundwave that travels through the rock, and we can see where the density of the rock changes along with sound refracted back at the microphones. These two methods working together can give a very good idea of what's underground.

We then find the oil shale layer, and find a place were it runs uninterrupted for a while, and then we drill down, and start drilling horizontally through the oil shale layer. The drill hole is cased, and through the horizontal section of the pipe there are holes that allow fluids through. Liquid is them pumped down into the casing.

The liquid is where things get interesting. Most drilling liquids are a mixture of various chemicals and diesel fuel. The diesel fuel mix is pumped down the drill hole and once it reaches it's ignition pressure it explodes, and the force of the explosion is driven out of the holes in the horizontal section of the pipe where it fractures the rock layer, freeing hydrocarbon gases and liquids from the rock matrix.

This method is horrible for the environment because you have to dispose of the diesel fuel mixture, and there is a serious risk of contaminating ground water when you pump it underground.

Some companies use liquid nitrogen though. The liquid nitrogen is pumped down, and where it comes into contact with the oil shale, the oil shale will destroy itself by contracting. (An interesting property of rock is that it is far easier to pull it apart than to smash it apart. Steel for instance has the same hardness regardless of what direction the pressure is being applied.) The hydrocarbons and the liquid nitrogen are brought up and the nitrogen is allowed to evaporate. Since our atmosphere is 70% nitrogen this method doesn't present an environmental problem.
